name: Fat grafting lips
lead: Lip fat grafting, also called autologous fat transfer, moves a person's own fat, usually taken by liposuction from another body area such as the abdomen, into the lips to add volume and shape. People choose it for a fuller, softer lip that does not use a synthetic filler, and because part of the result can persist longer than a hyaluronic acid filler. Wikipedia describes it as one of the better options for a semi-permanent result, with possible lumps or scarring.[1]

Fat transfer generally has three stages: harvesting, processing and reinjection [2]. Grafted fat can be partly reabsorbed, and weight change can alter the result [2]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source treated as unverified, gives one-year retention of roughly 50-70 percent and says repeat sessions are often needed [3].
Lip-specific clinical data were not found for this wiki; one registered trial in the sources concerns fat-derived cells for dry mouth, not lip appearance [4].

Surgical applications usually use general anaesthesia (per Wikipedia)[1]

paras: Fat is collected, purified and injected in small amounts into the lips [2][3]. Wikipedia lists it among lip augmentation options alongside hyaluronic acid fillers and implants [1].

Wikipedia places fat transfer within a wider group of lip augmentation approaches that aim to increase lip size, correct asymmetry, create protrusion or adjust the ratio between upper and lower lip.[1] Surgeons harvest fat through liposuction or excision from a site that can spare it and either inject it or place it surgically; Wikipedia says surgical applications usually involve general anaesthesia.[1] Because fat is the patient's own tissue, there is no foreign-material allergy risk, unlike products derived from animal collagen.[1]
Grokipedia says Gustav Neuber used fat injections in 1893 to correct scars and that Sydney Coleman standardised the technique in 1995 [3]. These dates come from an unverified source.

Wikipedia describes a sequence of materials used in lips: paraffin injections around 1900 that failed, liquid silicone from the early 1960s that was abandoned about thirty years later over concerns about health and long-term appearance, and injectable bovine collagen from about 1980, which required an allergy test and lasted weeks to months.[1] Later options include hyaluronic acid gels such as Restylane (778,000 injections in the US in 2006 per the American Society of Plastic Surgeons) and Juvederm, typically lasting six months or more, calcium hydroxylapatite, ePTFE implants such as Gore-Tex, and PMMA-containing fillers, some of which have been associated with nodules.[1]

Non-surgical temporary options include lip plumper cosmetics, which irritate the lip skin with ingredients such as capsaicin to cause swelling, and vacuum suction devices that cause temporary swelling.[1]

Wikipedia notes that fat transfer in general can be partly reabsorbed, with reports of up to 50 percent in breast augmentation, and that weight gain or loss can change the transferred fat [2]. Grokipedia reports lip retention of about 50-70 percent after a year and that surgeons may overcorrect by 20-30 percent [3].

General fat grafting complications listed by Wikipedia include swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain, scarring, infection and contour irregularities [2]. For lips, Wikipedia mentions lumps and scarring [1]. Wikipedia's lip augmentation article cautions that overfilled lips can look unnatural, that overaggressive injections can cause lumpiness and too little can leave ridges.[1]
Reported complications that apply to any lip augmentation include swelling, bruising and allergic or irritant reactions, with scarring and lumping as possible undesired cosmetic effects.[1]
No studies found. A registered phase 1/2 trial uses fat-derived stromal vascular cells for autoimmune dry mouth, which is a different purpose [4].

timeline.event: Gustav Neuber uses fat injections for scars (per Grokipedia).[3]
Sydney Coleman formalises fat grafting technique (per Grokipedia).[3]

card.summary: Your own fat injected into the lips; semi-permanent, with partial reabsorption reported.
card.note: Retention varies; no lip-specific trials found.

quick.overview:
Fat is taken from elsewhere on the body and injected into the lips to add volume.

It is described as longer lasting than temporary fillers, but part of the fat can be reabsorbed.
quick.mechanism: Fat is harvested, processed and injected in small amounts; surviving fat stays as lip volume.
quick.risks: Reported issues include swelling, bruising, lumps, scarring, uneven results and volume loss.

chain: Fat is harvested from the patient's own body
Processed fat is injected in small amounts into the lips
Surviving fat adds volume, shape and softness
angle.text: The surgeon places the patient's own fat into the upper and lower lips to add fullness or correct proportion. The portion of fat that takes in the lips remains as tissue, which is why the result is described as semi-permanent.
